description: We are ITIan, a team of AI & ML students at ITI in Egypt, taking part in NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026. Our shared skills are Python, machine learning, and presenting complex ideas clearly. We chose the challenge “Be an Earth System Trend Detective” and are building Trendoscope: a tool that uses NASA Earth data to show whether a change, such as in rainfall or temperature, is real or just random. We are excited to build, learn, and share our project with the Cairo community and globally.
summary:
Trendoscope is an interactive website that lets anyone investigate whether a climate variable in a region is truly changing, and understand the answer, in under three minutes. It is built around the Earth System Trend Detective challenge and uses NASA Earth data.

Users pick a region, time range, and variable (water, land, weather, or vegetation). A Python backend runs the trend analysis and returns a time-series graph, key statistics, and a plain-language verdict. A “Chance Machine” shuffles the data to show visually whether a trend is real or just random noise. Users can also compare two regions, play a detective-style game that links events such as floods to their possible causes, follow a kids’ story mode, and ask an LLM questions limited to the data. Demo cases focus on Egypt and the MENA region.

It addresses the challenge by turning raw satellite data into guided, trustworthy analysis that needs no statistics background. This matters because science only creates impact when it reaches the public. Trendoscope helps students and communities see climate change in their own region, and judge it with evidence rather than guesswork.
details:
Trendoscope turns NASA Earth observation data into a guided investigation. The user chooses a region (by dropdown or map), a time range, a resolution, and a variable (water, land, weather, or vegetation). A Python backend processes the data and runs a trend test. The site returns an interactive time-series graph, key statistics, and a plain-language “verdict” on whether the change is real. The “Chance Machine” shuffles the data many times to show visually whether the observed trend could happen by luck. Users can also compare two regions, play a detective game that links events such as floods to their possible causes, follow a kids’ story mode with a two-date slider and quiz, and ask an LLM questions restricted to the data.

Benefits and intended impact

A student with no statistics background can investigate a climate variable and understand the answer in under three minutes. We want climate evidence to reach the public, not just scientists, so people can judge changes in their own region (with demo cases for Egypt and MENA) from data rather than headlines.

Tools and technologies

  • Python, Jupyter, and pandas for data processing and trend analysis
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with Plotly.js for the interactive front end
  • GitHub for the repository, with GitHub Pages for hosting
  • An LLM, limited to the project’s data, for explanations and Q&A
  • Ubuntu laptops for development
  • AI tools to help build the website, demo video, and slides, as disclosed in our AI-use statement

How it is creative

  • A detective case-file theme with a verdict stamp
  • The Chance Machine, which makes statistical significance visible
  • A kids’ story mode and a detective game that make the data approachable
  • Avatar-style mascot powers for water, land, weather, and vegetation

Factors we considered

  • Validity: the verdict relies on a statistical test, and the LLM answers only from the data, to limit made-up claims
  • Accessibility: no statistics background required
  • Feasibility: a 24-hour hackathon with a four-person team and limited front-end experience, so we built a static website and added features in phases (core analysis, then comparison, then the LLM explainer)
  • Honesty about limits: we are transparent about what the data can and cannot show
